title: The Golden Goose
paragraphs: There was once a man who had three sons. The youngest was called Dummling,[1] and everyone despised him, mocked him, and sneered at him at every turn.
One day the eldest wanted to go into the forest to chop wood. Before he left, his mother gave him a lovely sweet cake and a bottle of wine, so that he wouldn’t go hungry or thirsty.

When he got to the forest, he met a little old man with gray hair, who wished him good day and said, “Please give me a piece of the cake in your pocket, and let me have a drink of your wine. I’m so hungry and thirsty.” But the clever son answered, “If I give you my cake and wine, I’ll have none left for myself. Get lost!” And he left the little man standing there and walked on.
But when he started chopping down a tree, it wasn’t long before he swung badly, and the axe cut into his arm, so that he had to go home and have it bandaged. And that was the little gray man’s doing.

Next, the second son went into the forest, and his mother gave him a cake and a bottle of wine, just as she had given the eldest. The little old gray man met him too and asked him for a piece of cake and a drink of wine. But the second son also said, quite sensibly, “Whatever I give you gets taken away from me. Get lost!” And he left the little man standing there and walked on. His punishment came quickly. After only a few blows at the tree, he struck himself in the leg and had to be carried home.

Then Dummling said, “Father, please let me go and cut wood.” His father answered, “Your brothers hurt themselves doing it. Leave it alone. You don’t know the first thing about it.” But Dummling begged for so long that finally his father said, “Oh, go on, then. You’ll learn something by hurting yourself.” His mother gave him a cake made with water and baked in the ashes, and a bottle of sour beer to go with it.

When he got to the forest, the little old gray man met him too, greeted him, and said, “Give me a piece of your cake and a drink from your bottle. I’m so hungry and thirsty.” Dummling answered, “All I have is ash-cake and sour beer. If that suits you, let’s sit down and eat.” So they sat down, and when Dummling took out his ash-cake, it had turned into a fine sweet cake, and the sour beer had become good wine. They ate and drank, and afterward the little man said, “Because you have a good heart and are willing to share what you have, I’ll give you some good luck. Over there stands an old tree. Cut it down, and you’ll find something among its roots.” Then the little man said goodbye.

Dummling went and cut down the tree, and when it fell, there in the roots sat a goose with feathers of pure gold. He picked her up, took her along, and went to an inn, where he planned to spend the night. Now, the innkeeper had three daughters. They saw the goose and were curious what kind of marvelous bird it could be, and each of them wished she had one of its golden feathers.
The eldest thought, “I’ll soon find a chance to pull out a feather.” As soon as Dummling had gone out, she grabbed the goose by the wing, but her finger and hand stuck fast to it.
The second came along soon afterward, thinking only of how to get a feather for herself, but she had barely touched her sister when she was held fast too.

Finally the third girl came along with the same idea, and the other two shrieked at her, “Stay away! For heaven’s sake, stay away!” But she had no idea why she should. “They’re over there,” she thought, “so I might as well be there too.” She ran up to them, and the moment she touched her sister, she was stuck fast. So all three had to spend the night beside the goose.

In the morning Dummling tucked the goose under his arm and went on his way, paying no attention to the three girls dangling from it. They had no choice but to keep running after him, veering left and then right, wherever his legs happened to take him.

Out in the middle of the fields they ran into the parson. Seeing the parade, he said, “Shame on you, you worthless girls! Why are you chasing this young man across the fields? Is that decent?” And with that he grabbed the youngest girl by the hand to pull her away. But the instant he touched her, he stuck fast too and had to run along behind.

Before long the sexton came by, and he was amazed to see his master, the parson, trotting after three girls. “Hey, your reverence!” he called. “Where are you off to in such a hurry? Don’t forget we have a christening today!” He ran up and caught the parson by the sleeve, and found himself held fast as well.

As the five of them trotted along in a line, two laborers carrying hoes came up from the fields. The parson shouted to them and begged them to pull him and the sexton loose. But they had barely touched the sexton when they stuck fast too, and now seven people were running behind Dummling and his goose.

Soon afterward he reached a city whose king had a daughter so solemn that nobody could make her laugh. The king had therefore issued a decree: whoever could make her laugh would marry her. When Dummling heard this, he went before the princess with his goose and its whole train. The moment she saw the seven people running on and on, one behind another, she burst out laughing, loudly, as if she would never stop. So Dummling asked to have her as his wife. But the king didn’t like the idea of him as a son-in-law and came up with all kinds of excuses. He said Dummling must first bring him a man who could drink a whole cellarful of wine. Dummling thought of the little gray man, who would surely be able to help. He went into the forest, and at the spot where he had cut down the tree he found a man sitting with a very sad face. Dummling asked him what was weighing so heavily on him, and the man answered, “I’m so thirsty, and nothing quenches it. I can’t stand cold water. I’ve just emptied a barrel of wine, but to me that was like a drop on a hot stone!”
“I can help you with that,” said Dummling. “Just come along with me, and you’ll get your fill.”

He took the man to the king’s cellar, and the man bent over the enormous barrels and drank and drank until his hips ached. Before the day was over he had emptied every barrel. Then Dummling asked again for his bride, but the king was annoyed that an ugly fellow whom everyone called Dummling should carry off his daughter, and he set a new condition: first Dummling must find a man who could eat a whole mountain of bread. Dummling didn’t stop to think. He went straight into the forest, and in the same place sat a man who was cinching a strap around his belly, pulling a terrible face, and saying, “I’ve eaten a whole ovenful of rolls, but what good is that to someone as hungry as I am? My stomach stays empty, and I have to tie myself up tight, or I’ll die of hunger.”

Dummling was delighted. “Get up and come with me,” he said. “You’ll eat until you’re full.” He brought him to the king’s palace, where all the flour in the entire kingdom had been gathered, and had a huge mountain of bread baked from it. The man from the forest planted himself in front of it and began to eat, and by the end of a single day the whole mountain was gone. For the third time Dummling asked for his bride, but again the king looked for a way out. This time he demanded a ship that could sail on land as well as on water. “Come sailing back in it,” he said, “and you shall have my daughter for your wife.”

Dummling went straight to the forest, and there sat the little gray man to whom he had given his cake. When the man heard what Dummling needed, he said, “You gave me food and drink, so I will give you the ship. I’m doing all this because you were kind to me once.” Then he gave him the ship that could sail on land and water. When the king saw it, he could no longer keep Dummling from marrying his daughter. The wedding was held, and when the king died, Dummling inherited his kingdom and lived happily with his wife for many years.
[1] Simpleton
